title: Dedaun Rimba: the first chapter of Kwasa Damansara.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #469 | DEDAUN RIMBA, KWASA DAMANSARA
excerpt: The first completed homes in a long-hyped master plan arrive with the roads, parks and MRT already finished — and with the compromises a townhouse always carries.
takeaways: Kwasa Damansara inverted the usual order: infrastructure, MRT and parks were completed before the first homes were handed over.
The strata landed format is what lets the architecture survive — common areas, facades and parking stay under management control.
The townhouse trade-offs are real: a narrow frontage, two staircases threaded through one structure, and a living room opening onto a public walkway.

sections.heading: A master plan that built the roads first
paragraphs: Sean opens standing in a township where the sequencing has been reversed. Roads, parks, street lighting, drainage, retention ponds and the MRT station are already finished and running; Dedaun Rimba is simply the first project to reach handover. He calls this the part the developer should be proud of, noting how rarely public transport arrives before the homes it is meant to serve.

The approach he describes is deliberate. The master developer built its own headquarters on site first as a show of commitment, completed the infrastructure, and only then parcelled out individual plots to different players — some landed, some high-rise, some mixed. Dedaun Rimba is the first of those to complete, with several more already under construction nearby.

In his episode notes Sean adds the honest caveat: for years the market was pessimistic about this site, and the change in perception really only came once the MRT stations were operating and the new highway had opened.

sections.heading: How Sean reads the groundwork
paragraphs: Before entering a single house, he walks the infrastructure — and this is the clearest example of the checklist he applies to any landed scheme. He looks at whether the road is properly premixed, where the manholes sit and what each serves: fibre, water, sewage, firefighting. He checks the drains, the pathways, and the planting between houses.

The feeder pillars get particular attention. These step power down from the main substation into the homes, so they must stay visible for maintenance while remaining an eyesore developers usually try to conceal. Here the solution is simply to paint them green, which Sean flags as one of the treatments he does not understand — landscape screening would have done the job better.

sections.heading: What a townhouse actually is
paragraphs: The scheme splits into terrace houses and townhouses, and the unit filmed is a one-and-a-half storey townhouse belonging to a viewer who invited Sean in. Two units share a single structure: one takes the lower floor, one the upper, each with its own entrance.

Sean is careful to separate this from a co-home, where each owner gets one flat floor and no staircase crosses into the other unit. In a townhouse the staircases intertwine within a shared structural frame, and the entrance is the real point of difference — narrow, with a lot of stairs. That, he says, is precisely why many buyers dislike the format.

The arrival sequence is compact but complete: premixed road to concrete apron, two tandem parking bays, then the utilities gathered together — water, electrical metering, doorbell, lighting, refuse chamber and a parcel area.

sections.heading: Inside the lower unit
paragraphs: The unit measures 1,396 sq ft, and its layout is deliberately unconventional. The kitchen sits at the front, immediately inside the entrance, while the living and dining spaces are pushed to the rear so they open onto the garden. Sean describes the experience as closer to high-rise living than to a conventional landed house, where you would normally enter the living hall first and find the kitchen at the back beside a service lane.

He notes the practical dimensions as he moves. The door clearance is a generous metre, but there is a step up into the unit he wishes were gentler. The entrance foyer is 1.48 m wide — enough that he questions whether a shoe cabinet will fit, and wishes for another 50 mm.

Inside, the ceiling drops to roughly 2.7 m over the entry zone before opening to about 3.1 m in the main space, with 600 mm floor tiles throughout. The unit had been handed over about a week earlier, so defect stickers are still scattered across the finishes and contractors are working in neighbouring homes.

sections.heading: Room by room, measured as he goes
paragraphs: The ground-floor bedroom — essential, Sean notes, for Asian families — is a comfortable size with a notably generous operable window. That window is also where he raises his sharpest concern: it opens directly onto a walkway that anybody can use, which makes curtains mandatory and raises a question about small children.

The bathrooms follow a modern logic he approves of. Rather than pushing the bathroom to the facade for natural ventilation, which would eat into both the living space's outlook and the bedroom's size, they sit inboard with mechanical ventilation panels and full-height tiling in the shower.

Upstairs, a first landing doubles as storage and accommodates the neighbouring unit's staircase; a second landing carries a roof access hatch and a ventilation system that pulls hot air out of the house — something Sean recommends for landed homes generally. The junior suite and master both sit under roughly 3.1 m ceilings, with the master running close to 4.8 m long, opening to a walk-in wardrobe and a balcony of about 1.9 m at its narrowest.

sections.heading: The park the houses face
paragraphs: The site plan is what makes the architecture work. Every house is single-loaded — one row only, with no back lanes sandwiched between two rows — so the central park becomes the piece everything addresses. Link houses ring the garden directly; townhouses sit on the outer ring.

Sean is candid that the link houses are the better product and were priced accordingly. They are effectively double the townhouse width, sit on higher ground, and enjoy more privacy: from the garden he can see straight into the townhouses but not into the link houses.

The landscape is doing real work. An earth mound integrates rock climbing, slides and rope climbing into two levels of play, and units are arranged organically to follow the topography rather than packed into maximum-yield rows — something he points out a yield-driven developer would never do.

sections.heading: A clubhouse kept deliberately small
paragraphs: The clubhouse is restrained and Sean means that as praise. The pool is a simple stretch with a gentle infinity edge, finished in pale blue and white rather than the usual dark mosaic, giving it what he calls a Santorini feel. The gym holds a handful of machines and a free-weight zone, sized for a development of only about 264 units.

His argument is that restraint is a maintenance decision. Elaborate water play areas and extravagant landscaping are expensive to run, and in his episode notes he makes the link explicit: the team did not go all out on design precisely so that maintenance fees stay under control. He rates the material choices highly — spray-painted finishes, stone-look tiles, angled columns and punched shading profiles that reward anyone who looks closely.

sections.heading: The price argument, and the strata case
paragraphs: The owner tells Sean he paid around RM780,000 at launch, roughly three years before filming. Sean treats that as the crux: a strata landed home from a reputable developer, under RM800,000, in the Klang Valley, within walking distance of a public park and an MRT station, is genuinely rare. Those figures reflect the recording date and one specific unit — present-day prices need fresh evidence.

He is equally clear about what that money now competes with. A similar layout in a condo can cost about the same, the site is leasehold while land next door is freehold, and the debate against a link house in an established township is a real one.

The strata format is his strongest structural argument. Because a maintenance fee covers boundaries, landscape, security and cleanliness, the facade survives intact instead of each owner painting their own colours and adding fences within the first week. Parking disputes go to management rather than to neighbours, and there is dedicated visitor parking — protections an individual-title scheme simply cannot offer.

pros: The master plan was activated in the right order — roads, parks, street lighting, walkways and a running MRT station were all completed before the first homes were handed over, with the developer building its own headquarters on site to show commitment.

The strata landed format keeps the scheme coherent: common areas, facades, security and parking stay under management, and the single-loaded site plan lets every home address a central garden instead of a back lane.

The design flair is consistent with the team's earlier work at KLPAC, Fennel, Capers and Danau — restrained landscaping, considered material textures and subtle structural detailing rather than showpiece facilities.
cons: The township will take years to finish and has no commercial component yet, so residents lean on Kota Damansara for amenities while paying close to what a similar condo layout costs.

Some treatments puzzle him — feeder pillars painted green rather than screened with planting, and a lower-floor living room opening directly onto a public landscape walkway, which he reads as a privacy and security question.
The townhouse format carries its own penalties: a narrow frontage, two staircases threaded through one structural system, and outer-ring units facing unusually wide roads.

closing: Dedaun Rimba's real argument is not the house but the order things were built in. Whether it suits you depends on how much you value a finished master plan and a strata-managed street over the width and freehold title a link house elsewhere would give you for similar money.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full public English captions and his published YouTube episode notes. Measurements, unit size and the purchase price are as stated in the video and reflect the recording date. The 3 on 3 section paraphrases the three things Sean says he likes and the three he has concerns about, presented near the end of the episode.
